lead: Every line of code in a flight computer is a safety decision. A wrong altitude on a display, a missed spoiler command, a badly tuned fly-by-wire gain — each can end a flight. RTCA DO-178B is the industry guide that makes a software team prove its work: that requirements were written, that code matches them, and that tests show the code does what the requirements say. Regulators accept it as one acceptable way to show airborne software is safe, so most civil avionics suppliers follow it closely.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.2 on IMA and partitioning, plus some familiarity with software testing. Only a few universities teach this topic.

sections.h3: The V-model: decompose down, verify up

blocks.text: RTCA DO-178B, Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification (1992), is industry guidance, not law. Regulators accept it as one acceptable means of showing that airborne software is safe; its European twin is EUROCAE ED-12B. It describes a life cycle shaped like a V.

The left arm decomposes. Aircraft requirements become high-level requirements (HLR): what the software must do, with no design. HLRs become low-level requirements (LLR): algorithms, data flows, logic. LLRs become source code.

The right arm verifies. Unit tests check code against LLRs. Integration tests check that modules work together. Validation checks the finished software against the aircraft requirements. Reviews and analyses count as verification too; DO-178B never says test only.

Traceability holds the V together, in both directions. Every HLR traces down to LLRs and to at least one test. Every LLR traces down to source code and to at least one test. A requirement with no test is a gap. Every test of a required behaviour must trace to a requirement; robustness tests of abnormal inputs are expected and are not traced to requirements. Auditors read the trace first.
The software level comes from the failure condition of the function, decided in the system safety assessment — not from the size or difficulty of the code.

blocks.text: Objectives scale with the level: level A carries the full set, level D only a small subset, level E none. At level A the structural coverage objective demands MC/DC (modified condition/decision coverage): every condition inside a decision must be shown to change that decision on its own, so a condition hidden by short-circuit evaluation is caught.
Plans, standards, configuration management and quality assurance records are objectives in their own right: who wrote the code, which version flew, who checked it.

spec.title: DO-178B V-model (top-to-bottom view)
spec.aria: Flow from aircraft requirements down through high-level and low-level requirements and code, then to unit test, integration test and validation.

examples.question: A spoiler control function is classified catastrophic, so its software is level A. Its requirements database holds 40 low-level requirements. A traceability review finds tests traced to 38 of them. (a) Find the requirement-to-test traceability percentage. (b) State how many gaps remain. (c) State whether the certification evidence is complete.
steps: Level: catastrophic failure condition gives software level A.
Total low-level requirements = 40; traced to tests = 38.
Gaps = 40 − 38 = 2 requirements with no traced test.
95% is below 100%, so the evidence is incomplete; each gap must be closed by a traced test, or the requirement removed with justification, before certification.
examples.answer: Traceability is 95%, with 2 requirements untraced, so the evidence is incomplete and the gaps must be closed.
examples.check:
traced = 38
total = 40
print(traced / total * 100)
print(total - traced)

traps: DO-178B prescribes no language, compiler or tool; it asks for evidence that objectives are met. A new compiler is allowed if you can show it does no harm.
Level follows the failure condition of the function, not the complexity, size or cost of the code.
Verification asks 'did we build it right' (code against requirements); validation asks 'did we build the right thing' (software against aircraft requirements).
Traceability is bidirectional. Answers that only trace requirement to test lose marks.
DO-178B is guidance accepted by regulators, not law; do not write that it is a legal requirement.

quiz.q: Who issues RTCA DO-178B and what is its title?
quiz.a: RTCA, a US industry body; title: Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification.

quiz.q: Name the failure condition for software levels A and E.
quiz.a: Level A: catastrophic. Level E: no safety effect.

quiz.q: Why must traceability run in both directions?
quiz.a: Upward trace proves every line of code exists for a stated requirement; downward trace proves every requirement has code and a test, so nothing is missing and nothing is extra.

quiz.q: A level C function has 60 low-level requirements; 54 have traced tests. Find the traceability percentage and the number of gaps.
A decision reads if (a and b) or c. Name the conditions that MC/DC must show changing the outcome.
quiz.a: The three conditions a, b and c; each must be shown to flip the decision on its own while the others stay fixed.

quiz.q: A team wants to fly level A software written in a new language with a new code generator. What does DO-178B require?
quiz.a: Nothing is banned. The team must meet the level A objectives for the code, including structural coverage to MC/DC, and supply evidence that the generator and tools do not insert errors.

quiz.q: A team completed all unit tests successfully but built the wrong altitude law. Which V-model step failed, and why would testing alone not catch it?
quiz.a: Validation failed: the software matched its requirements, but the requirements did not match the aircraft. Unit tests compare code to LLRs, so a wrong requirement passes every test below it.

beyond: Not for the exam. DO-178C replaced DO-178B in 2011 and adds supplements: DO-330 for tool qualification, DO-331 for model-based development, DO-332 for object-oriented software and DO-333 for formal methods. Industry keeps the trace in a requirements tool, and the auditor walks it electronically rather than on paper. Search for 'DO-178C supplements' and 'MC/DC coverage' for the modern picture.
